title: Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™
text: A couple of thoughts after just beating the main game. + The meat of this game lies within the nemesis system. It brings a lot of personality to the orcs on board, especially in the first couple of hours of playing. Orcs tend to remember quite a bit about past battles and taunt you with it on your return. Also there's a ranking system in which orcs get more powerful and gain more treats to take heed of. You might (depending on your skills and choices) find yourself fighting one orc for half of the game, making the term nemesis a real thing. + Graphically this game looks awesome, great atmosphere completely in tune with the movies. Animations are done really well and I just love the orc design in general. +- Gameplay is good most of the time with fluid movements and fighting system. But it is not without its flaws. Sometimes you keep on grabbing the wrong orc by the throat even when you're aiming a different direction, sometimes you just keep clinging to walls in a very unnatural way, climbing down or jumping down sometimes won't work as intended. These situations don't nearly happen often enough to make the game unbearable though, combat and navigating feels quite satisfying most of the time. +- The story feels scattered and not quite as solid as it would be if the game would be more linear. It is literally all over the place from time to time, and there isn't enough to it to make it feel coherent. + The voice acting is great though. + Also it is fun to stumble upon some more LOTR lore, with a little suspension of disbelief it's still entertaining and not too far fetched (just a little in the main story, especially towards the end). +- I'm not quite sure why Gollum was there at all, except for fanserving purpose. But again, he was voiced and animated perfectly so it was still convincing enough for me anyway. +- I was kinda hoping for at least one more map, but at least there are two that do look great. Udûn is my favorite by far, that is how I remember Mordor looking. The other map is a bit too generic and lush for my taste, although that is actually part of the lore so it does make some sort of sense. Both maps seem on the small side seeing you just can run from one end to the other within five minutes, but at least that makes it easier to finish I guess. And hey, plenty of collectibles and you can easily pick them up while on a mission if you want to. - The game difficulty could be a bit harder though, or maybe a lot. At least optionally.  Towards the end everything becomes a bit repetitive and without challenge. - The last few missions are quite disappointing as well both in terms of difficulty and -to a smaller degree- story. All in all there's a lot of fun to have in Shadow of Mordor and I would fully recommend it. I hope Shadow of War will be more coherent and challenging, although I've read the DLC might provide some challenge as well. I'll try that later though, I need a short break from all the button mashing for a couple of days right now ;)

title: Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™
text: Up front, my playtime represents a comprehensive playthrough of the base game to include all collectibles, side missions, and several achievements. If you're a fan of games like Batman (the combat is very familiar), God of War, Mark of Kri, and Conan, but want a dash of the "open world" then you will feel right at home here. The combat is great, the controls are smooth and intuitive, and the way you can shape some of the military hierarchy within the ranks of Uruk armies is a refreshing system that makes the game interesting and unique to its genre. The duality of the main character(s) is implemented very well and the game makes good use of the strengths they have to offer. The period in which SoM is set is also pretty interesting and fans of LotR will be absolutely giddy inside playing this. The collectibles and dialogue all made me want to watch the movies and read the books again. The minor downsides were that some of the missions did feel repetitive after awhile, primarily the outcasts ones where you are rescuing slaves over and over. There are 24 of those if I recall correctly and they never really change. They are optional though. Combat is a blast and you are given a variety of tools with which to dispatch your foes. This was great fun but also meant the game was never really much of a challenge and by the end I felt absolutely godlike. I spent somewhere around $7 on this game while it was on sale and received the GotY edition. I highly recommend it even at full price and am looking forward to playing through the additional content.

title: Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™
text: I really don't play much in the "brawler" category, but from the little I've seen, Monolith really did their homework. "Shadow Of Mordor" only has one gameplay loop, when it really comes down to it. Sure, there's a stealth "subloop" that you can get into, but in the end, the game always comes down to how you enter and exit a chain of dispatching orcs in up-close combat. Monolith got that experience extremely "right," mostly by way of their skill progression system. There's an almost magical balance between the combat remaining an interesting challenge while Talion grows more and more powerful. In my playthrough, things got noticeably easier as time went on, but it never got too easy or too rote. There are a lot of skills that you can weave together for maximum benefit, and "Shadow" is pretty decent at rewarding mastery, at least in the immediate sense. The downside of all that Talion can do is that the game sometimes struggles to figure out what you want. It never became a scourge, but there were still plenty of instances where Talion wouldn't, say, climb up a wall, because the combat system was telling him that "spacebar" meant "dodge" when I wanted "climb." In that same vein, I was sometimes a little perplexed about what Talion would and would not tackle vertically - some walls that clearly looked like giant collections of handholds actually weren't, apparently. (This is a bit jarring when your super-rad wraith-ranger can climb almost anything, but then arbitrarily says, "Nope, can't climb that thing which looks like it would incredibly easy. Sorry.") The "Nemesis" System is an interesting idea that does play well, but it has a couple of problems. First, as it turns out, there's only so much actual meat on that bone. At first, the constantly self-replacing cast of procedurally-generated baddies is pretty nifty. Later on, though, you start to shrug your shoulders as you realize that what you're doing isn't having any real, permanent effect on what's going on. At some point, when you're highly (or totally) upgraded and have all the runes you want, hammering away at one more Uruk Captain doesn't mean anything. Second, the Nemesis System has a noticeable penchant for cooking up opponents who are actually tougher than high-level story encounters. There were some regular captains that emerged that caused me far more trouble than Sauron's Black Captains, the supposed terrors of Mordor. (They're actually rather a gang of pushovers, if you ask me.) Once you've faced a high-damage, quick-firing, ranged-attack orc who's immune to all regular damage, a big bad who hits hard (but slowly) and is taken down by moves that are easy to pull off is a bit of a let-down. ...and the ending isn't much of a payoff. I don't want to spoil it, but I will say it's abrupt and offers almost nothing in the way of closure. It's sort of reminiscent of "Mass Effect 3," where you get this nagging feeling that the developer ran out of money, time, and ideas when it was time to actually plonk a climactic capstone on their experience. Story-wise, Monolith does a nice job with giving you collectibles that trickle juicy bits of lore down to you, but I found myself wishing that the various characters would have gotten more "airtime" instead. So, do play "Shadow Of Mordor." Just play it for the mid-game instead of the end.

title: Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™
text: Overall, SOM is an OK game, 3 out of 5 stars.  The story just isn't that compelling unless you're SUPER into Tolkein.  The combat system is great, because it's basically the Arkham games system, which is great.  However, unlike the Arkham games, SOM is too overpowered.  In the Arkham games yeah you collected gadgets and techniques, but it wasn't to be a supreme fighter, it was to counteract the new enemy types that couldn't be taken down by standard punches and kicks.  In SOM, there really isn't a variety of enemies, and the few that they are, can still be taken down easily by the standard moves.  That's why the added abilities just makes the main character OP in my opinion.  The animations are fantastic, always get to see a cool way for an Uruk to die.  The challenges and the discoverable items were boring, again, unless you're SUPER into Tolkein.  Take Tomb Raider, when you find something, it's engaging, and has to do with the story, in SOM they're just there for the sake of finding them mostly.  Basically from a cutscene, animation, fighting system standpoint, the game is great, but the meat and potatoes of it as a whole fell through.  Blah story, almost no chance of ever dying or feeling a real threat to your life.  The nemesis system is cool in theory, and actually works out pretty well, but without that actual fear of dying and therefore stacking the nemesis system against you due to your failure, it too falls short.  Get it on sale like I did, not worth full price, but it is worth a try.

title: Might & Magic X - Legacy
text: I really want to like this game. I even want to beat it. But I can't do either and here's why. Even though this is not like Might and Magics of old (6, 7, and 8), at its core, it is still an enjoyable game with decent music, customizable  character classes, and a fairly rich fantasy world. I dare say, as a concept, it may even be worthy of being among some of the best dungeon crawlers out there. The problem is, It's just not playable. Mac, PC, high graphics, or none, the game is unstable and getting it to work is an absolute chore. I have restarted it at least 30 times, had to reload 5 different saves, and have turned my graphics down to nothing, and it STILL crashes at portal screens, opening chests, or even walking around a forest. The game just isn't optimized, for ANY system, and though you can brute force your way through the crashes, it REALLY takes its tole on your patience. For the asking price of $30, it's an absolute insult. As Limbic and Ubisoft are no longer supporting this title, this is a buyer beware review, with "purchase at your own risk" tacked on. If you want to try, and try to enjoy the game for what it is (despite the crashes) then for the love of whatever deity you follow, or not, at least wait for a sale. You'll be sorry if you don't.

title: Might & Magic X - Legacy
text: I was set on not recommending this during my first few hours of gameplay. It didn't feel like a bad game, but also didn't feel like a good one either. After Legend of Grimrock it just felt so much more shallow and silly and ... just.. not as good. I still don't think it can compare to Legend of Grimrock, but after having put many more hours into it - it grew on me enough to give it a good review. Why is it not as good? Well, the story is not as enticing, the puzzles are less interesting, the upgrades are less exciting, too much clutter loot, and overall not as well-designed. It's designed well enough, but there are plenty of large areas that are there just to waste your time moving through them, while they actually bring no benefit to the game (no monsters to fight, no secrets to find). But despite all that the game still offers plenty of enjoyment. Combat system is turn based, so you have time to control every character without rushing. Leveling up is rewarding, it is possible to make a badass character who can take regular-enemy life bars out in 3-4 hits. There are plenty of spells to cast, weapons to use, armors to put on. There are rings, amulets, potions, buffs, debuffs. Level up system is decent, with both attribute and skill increases. Not every class/race has access to the same tiers of skills, but a lot of them have access to most skills in general, which is nice. For example a mage may not start with a dodge or crossbow skill or be able to advance to a grandmaster level of those, but he can still get to an Expert level. Towns are pretty large with many NPCs, (if you're into that. I'm not, but i appreciate the effort developers put into this.) All in all it's not an amazing game, but it still deserves a positive review because it is well made, and it is actually kind of fun (the battles anyway. i'm all about the battles.) And after you've played through Legend of Grimrock three times and unlocked all the achievements and just don't want to play it anymore but still want something like it - Might and Magic X one is an acceptable substitute.

title: Might & Magic X - Legacy
text: Might and Magic X is an ok game that falls short of pretty much all its successors (the word is correct, as technically, MMX is supposed to be something like MM 5.5, hence why you get MM6 to complement it), even the mediocre Might and Magic 9. As if to add insult to injury, UbiSoft gives us the extremely good MM6 as a part of the deal as if to tell you - here, this is what Might and Magic 6 represented - tons of spells, water walking, flight, exploration, the ability to look under every nook and cranny and actually be rewarded for it. Might and Magic 6-8 were the golden years of the franchise, and every game brought the lineage to new hights. Then came MM9 which pretty much destroyed all the exploration, but added new 3D engine and interesting locales with roughly as much freedom as its forefathers. And now, as a slap in the face comes MMX Legacy with its MM6 bonus. Let's compare the two: 1. Movement. 1.1. MM6 has free movement, turning, water walking, flight, strategic positioning even while entering combat AND during combat. 1.2. MMX is rigid as hell. You are forced into a square grid which not only makes the whole movement experince choppy and unpleasant, but also forces you to turn around just as choppily just to see if you haven't missed anything. Why were can't I enter water squares without having a certain god's blessing? Did people simply forget what a Water Walk spell is? 2. Combat. 2.1. MM6 has the best of both systems - turn based combat and real time combat. Turn based combat works like MMX, while in real time you could fly, play to the enemies' disadvantages (like use Water Walk and escpe on water while range attacking the enemies). It was liberating as hell and actually encouraged strategic thinking. 2.2. MMX combat is rigid and there is little need for strategy. Battles are best won if you can put yourself in a corner or a corridor so that only a few enemies at a time have the opportunity to attack you, while you pick them off easily as the others simply wait dumbly for their turns to enter your killzone. And people said that flying and water walking in MM6-8 was exploiting the system... 3. Exploration. 3.1. MM6 encouraged exploration on any level and at any time and actually rewarded you for it. And to prove that, the devs actually put a flight scroll in your starting city, so that you can go and explore. Opening every inch of a map in MM6 is exciting and rewards you with secret islands off the coast that have money or chests lying around, craters in mountains with obelisks, chests, and other rewards. I even found extremely rare items like artifacts and relics in such chests! Even if you encounter difficullt enemies (like even dragons or titans), you have a chance to fly or teleport away to escape and come back later. 3.2. MMX offers little in terms of exploration, mainly because everything is a corridor - and even if you get adventurous and press on, you get punished by it, because you encounter very difficult enemies and have little or no chance against them, which results in death. Artifacts and Relics are found in specific location, and up until now with 2 running play-throughs with 2 different groups, I found the same artifacts in the very same spots in the very sam dungeons. YAY! 4. Equipment. 4.1. MM6 has tons of gear diversity. You would just bite your nails before opening a chest or looting a body, looking at that hotbar right above your characters. Ding... You find 24 gold and an item (Axe)! - hell yeah, my guy needs a new one, is it better? Ding... You found 1096 gold and an item (Relic)! OH YEAH!!! What does it do? Can I even identify it? Can any of guys use it? OH it's a ring, all of my guys can use rings, but I don't know what it does! Screw that, I am porting to town to find out! This nailbiting, mouthwatering experience is very much gone in MMX. 4.2. MMX has a very rigid gear system. 90% of the time I have been finding better stuff in shops than in chests or the bodies of slain enemies. If you want to make a specific character build, you have to rely on the shops in the various cities. And yeah, just go to that same dungeon to get your artifact at the end. YAY... 5. Characters and classes. MMX does have more diversity in Race/Class creation than MM6 (12 vs 9), but one can't escape the feeling that many of those race/class combos play and feel the same. They also reuse the MM6 system of making specialized fighters & casters, and then add hybrids of both classes. So in essense, you have 4 warrior classes, 4 Hybrid classes and 4 Caster classes. One nukes more, another heals more. One gets an extra attack, the other is better protected. Hybrids can really accomplish a lot and supplement your party well. A touch and go system, really... In MM6 you had limitations - you Cleric was a poor fighter, but could heal and learn Light/Dark Magic and become an even better healer, buffer, or nuker. Your Knight could wear the best armor and hit like a ten ton truck, and get more attacks per turn. Your Paladin (the Knight/Cleric combo) could hit and heal, but had no access to the best healing & buffing spells from the light tree. Here, you get a Crusader with Lay on Hands for max heals at any given time at the cost of all your mana who can learn Grandmaster Light Magic (cool heals/buffs), Grandmaster Sword (good fighter), Grandmaster Heavy (well protected), Grandmaster Arcane (Lots of magic resistance). Why not have a few of those in your party, then? IMO, Crusaders very much break the game. 6. To conclude: please don't get me started on the UDONTPLAY 3rd party DRM... EDIT: As I put it in the comment: That being said, I am a completionist and I will still finish the game. I, however, cannot shake the feeling that it is inferior to all others though. It is like returning to the dark times before your golden age just for the sake of nostalgia. In short, I would recommend that you buy an MM6-8 bundle and immerse yourself in the 3D-ish world of those games. Explore, fly, walk on water, steal stuff and have fun. Don't be swayed by this Grimrock-style Might and Magic game just because of the Might and Magic in it like I was...

title: Might & Magic X - Legacy
text: First and foremost this game is RETRO!!! Which means all you noob gamers weened on skyrim and all the fancy flashy graphics and refined systems of modern day gaming...get over yourself and pay homage to history. I played World of Xeen back in the 90s when it first came out, and since then have played every Might and magic game I could, including the heroes games and every spin off etc. I mention Xeen specifically because this game is basically the great gand child of that game and all the games to come between then and now were just pretenders to the throne. I do my homework, I read every publication of every review for every game I buy without fail, I start with meta critic and work my way down the list via thier links. And every mouth breathing tard wanting to put down a few black and white pixels about the shortcomings of this game obviously missed the point of RETRO!!! Forget the reviews dont listen to the nay sayers every single part of this game was made intentionally, the grid system the combat, the OP enemies early on. Its all about the ambiance, and the history and the very concept of a game of this ilk. Its funny too cause you read reviews on games that scream RETRO!!!! fromt he start and they are considered masterpieces of old school gaming and should be admired for thier edgy psuedo-historical content. title: Might & Magic X - Legacy
text: Hello, here is my review of Might & Magic X - Legacy: first off there is no free modding kit like advertised in the shop. To use the mod kit you have to download UnityPro, after 30 days unityPro costs 1500$ once or 75$ per month to use. 32 bit users are getting screwed because they have no sound effects and are reduced to middle grafic settings. So false advertising at work in the shop. It uses Ubisoft launcher as second layer of drm, isnt it fun? Problems with your internet connection? Bad luck you will not be able to play it. The technical aspect of the game is horrible. On 32 bit system the game is incomplete, you get only middle textures, no party sounds, no monster sounds and other features are missing. The overall performance is bad. On 64 bit you get hight textures, animations and all but it does not look too good at all. That would be tolerable, roleplaying games are mostly about gameplay and not super grafic quality. But the performance is supbar compared to the grafic quality delivered. It runs really choppy and many systems. Even on the latest 780 gforce power rigs it does not run smooth so that is that. Performancewise it is a catastrophe. Gameplay: 12 classes Defender, Bladedancer, Ranger, Mecenary , Freemage, Shaman, Druid, Runepriest, Barbarian, Scout, Crusader. Unfortunately ranged classes like the ranger and scout are useless farther into the game. You have very little opportunity to fight monsters at range, in melee they do next to no damage, because the main ranged stat perception does not improve the damageoutput of melee much. The Ranger gets a point blank shot, this does not really help to improve his damage output. Magic classes are strong until the monsters get rediculous high resistance against their magic school. Most monster are resistent against a magic school or general resistent against all magic, so tough luck if your chosen magic school like fire or wind does nothing against that special pack of monsters or the boss. Magic user tend to burn your mana potion resources like mana addicts. Defender, Bladedance and Crusader perform very good, the blade dancer with daggers buffed up by crusader spells is the best damage dealer in the game by a wide margin. He is so op that it brakes the whole class system. You will struggle without a bladedancer or barbarian as damage dealer in your party. The whole class system is borked and unbalanced The combat relies very much on luck and potion chucking, It does not feel very might and magic like in the later stages of the game. With a suboptimal(no bladedancer or two)  party you get one tough as nails fight after the other, in m&m series the game would throw many easy monsters at you to test your resource managementskills and use of aid spells, but not one hard battle after the other. The pacing is frustrating and not fun even on the easier adventurer mode. The encounterdesign is not good, it is one overly hard battle after the other, even for trash monsters. There is no respawn, the monster count is too low to succed by grinding. M&m x is the only rpg i know where i can't win through overleveling, so for me it is no rpg at all. Leveling your character through grinding, getting better equipment, farming gold, leveling skills is what makes a good rpg for me. the skill system is more might and magic like. It is very rudimental and easy. You have 4 skillpoints per level to invest in your skills, after 7 15 20 skillpoints you can upgrade to a new skilltier, expert, master, grandmaster, you will get boni for each upgrade. Some skills are more powerfull then others. So magic skills get 5% 10% 15% spell penetration and more resistance against that magic school while the infamous dagger skill gets expert 1 extra attack and plus hitrate, and on grand master 2 extra attacks and plus hitrate. Combined with dual whield skill you can get a staggering amount of 6 attacks per round, your bladedancer becomes a weapon of mass destruction. Compared to this all other skills and magic school are just a joke in terms of damageoutput. You will need some skills/spells to progress like protection against status ailments, healing spells but for raw damage dagger and dual whield is greater then none. Per levelup you get 4 attribute points you can allocate where you wish. For a seasoned rpg player it should be easy to get a deasant build. Melee 2 strength 1 perc, 1 vit, magic 1 magic, 1 vit 2 spirit in the beginning and 2 magic 1 vit 1 spirit later when you have enough manapoints (never). I think the game release was rushed, the gameplay is boring and frustrating, the encounters are onesided against the player to the extreme, you cannot grind in a rpg!, the performance is bad even for the grafics and on excellent gaming rigs, the skills, classes, monster encounters are not balanced at all. I do not recommend this game. Have a nice day

title: Mini Metro
text: Here is proof you don't need Unity5 to make a GREAT game. It looks a little like the 1970's Atari tennis - but with colour and  A LOT more little blocks moving around. It is essentially a join the dots resource management game - which sounds demeaning but it is not, this is a challenging, fun and addictive game. As the player you get a number of locomotives, carriages, lines and few other goodies with which to build an efficient underground/subway/U-Bahn in a variety of large ciities across Europe, Asia, America and Africa. Passengers mass at stations. They want to go to other stations that match their shape (triangulasr passengers want to go to traingular stations), easy enough but there are quite a few shapes. If to many passengers crowd a station the whole transport system collapses - game over. To move these people you put locomotives on the line, busy lines may mean you have to place extra locos (up tp 4 per line) going in both directions. You only have a limited number of lines and locos which have limited space so.....well you know how these things work. Intersecting train lines, tunnels under rivers and the appearance of specialised stations (hospitals for example) add to the challenge. It's all about getting people out of the system quickly so you can load the next one onto a train and get rid of him to. The problem is the more efficient your train system, the more peole want to use it, so.....well you know how these things work. More stations appear on the map over time, meaning at times a total redesign of track routes etc may be needed. The game is not finished (for example as of writing this, audio is not quite ready), but it is stable and VERY playable - but as I said one of those addicitive 'I'll play just a bit longer" games that ends up filling your evening.

text: Mini Metro is a mini strategy puzzle game. The idea is to link up stations so commuters can get to there destination. The longer you are in the game the more demanding the commuters become and this is where you need to place you railway lines strategically. The games concept is simple but can get difficult quickly. This makes each game you play short and sweet. It is fun and can be addictive, trying to better your high score each time. The graphics are simple but effective for a game like this. title: Mini Metro
text: Great fun: simple yet challenging. Since the levels have a certain randomness, no level plays out exactly the same. This gives a nice replay-value! PS: To get the achievements sometimes one truly has to push the limits, micro-manage single trains, etc.... and/or just have luck (due to the random element of each run/level). PPS: Not sure whether the full price is justified, but so far multiple cities have been made available (for free) after the initial release (and of course bugfixes too).... Thx to the developers!

text: The game only consists of three simple puzzle mechanics. You have to complete 25 puzzles of each kind. They all feel nice and novel for the first five puzzles, but after that it's just boring. At this point, you may just think that puzzle games aren't my cup of tea. However, I'm fond of games such as Picross, Sudoku, LYNE and so on, so it's not that. I don't know what make Missing Translation fails, but it does. I'm in the last set of puzzles, and I don't even have the will to finish the game. Plus, I'm a bit frustrated at how the title has absolutely nothing to do with the game (I studied Languages in college and was delighted to see a game about language barriers and/or communication). So yeah, for once, I won't recommend a free game.
